food.text: Sangam literature, dated from the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE, offers some of the early references to food and recipes in South India. Culinary historians K. T. Achaya and Ammini Ramachandran point to it as a window on how people ate in that age.

Indian Ocean trade spread Indian spices to the western world during the classical era. Black pepper, cinnamon and cardamom, along with fragrant woods like sandalwood and agarwood, were part of the Indo-Roman trade network.

The Silk Road, a network of land and sea routes used from 130 BCE, carried goods, diseases and ideas between East and West, including between China and India. Chinese merchants sent silks, rice and crockery, while Indian merchants sent a plethora of influential spices.
The poet Avvaiyar described her hearty summer lunch as steamed rice, smoked and mashed aubergine and tangy frothy buttermilk. It is a simple meal of the kind Sangam poets set down in verse.
The poet Mudathama Kanniyar described a royal lunch he was treated to in the palace of the Chola king. It included skewered goat meat, crispy fried vegetables, rice and over 16 varieties of dishes.
The ancient port of Muziris on India's southwestern coast was a hub of the Indo-Roman spice trade. Black pepper is native to the nearby Malabar Coast, where it is still extensively cultivated.
Sangam literature mentions food eaten on several different types of leaf platters and on thalis with multiple bowls. The thali, still a familiar way of serving a meal, appears in these early texts.

The Silk Road exchange left its mark on kitchens in both countries. Ginger, cinnamon and black pepper are present in various Chinese culinary styles, and rice dishes cooked in Indianized Chinese woks are found in southern India.

Sangam period archaeological sites such as Tirunelveli have uncovered household bronzeware, including ornamental vase stands, bowls, jars and cups with ornamental bowl lids. These were likely used for thali presentation, as the Sangam texts describe.

art.text: Much early Indian architecture was built in wood or brick, which almost always decayed, burned, or was carried off for reuse. Because of this, rock-cut architecture, which began around 250 BCE, is especially important. Much of it clearly copies forms from contemporary buildings of which no examples remain.

Gandhara art is believed to have produced the first representations of Gautama Buddha in human form, ending the early period of aniconism in Buddhism. It combined Buddhist subject matter with the idealistic realism of Hellenistic art. The first surviving devotional images of the Buddha were created in the 1st to 3rd centuries AD under the Kushan Empire.

India has more than 1,500 known rock-cut structures, and Indian rock-cut architecture is more varied and abundant than any other form of rock-cut architecture in the world. Many contain artwork of global importance and are adorned with exquisite stone carvings. Seen from one angle, a rock-cut structure is a decorated rock quarry, since most of the removed stone was put to economic use elsewhere.

The Ajanta Caves in Maharashtra are rock-cut cave monuments dating back to the second century BC. They contain paintings and sculpture considered masterpieces of both Buddhist religious art and universal pictorial art.

The oldest rock-cut architecture is found in the Barabar caves in Bihar, personally dedicated by Ashoka around 250 BC. The extremely hard granite was cut in geometrical fashion and polished to a mirror-like finish. The caves show an amazing level of technical proficiency.

Stupas were soon richly decorated with sculptural reliefs, with early attempts at Sanchi Stupa No.2 in 125 BCE. Full-fledged sculptural decoration and scenes from the life of the Buddha followed at Bharhut (115 BCE), Bodh Gaya (60 BCE) and Mathura. Sanchi's toranas and then Amaravati (1st to 2nd century CE) came later.

The Great Stupa at Sanchi was thought to be founded by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka around 273 to 232 BCE. During the Shunga Dynasty (c. 150 to 50 BCE) it was enlarged to its present diameter of 120 feet. It was covered with a stone casing, topped with a balcony and umbrella, and encircled with a stone railing.

Mauryan art combined indigenous Indian traditions with distinct influences from ancient Persia and the Hellenistic world, as shown by the Pataliputra capital. The Maurya Empire flourished from 322 BCE to 185 BCE and controlled most of the subcontinent. This expansion facilitated a profound artistic and cultural synthesis.

Early Indian architecture was made from wood, which did not survive because of rotting and unstable structures. The earliest surviving examples are instead rock-cut architecture, including many Buddhist, Hindu and Jain temples.

The mirror-like polishing of the Barabar caves was abandoned and never revived, and neither the Karla Caves (1st century CE) nor the Ajanta Caves (5th century CE) are polished. This may be because Mauryan caves were sponsored by the imperial government, with huge resources. Later caves were largely the result of donations by commoners, who could not afford as much.

The Masarh lion, found near the Maurya capital of Pataliputra, is carved in Chunar sandstone with a polished finish, like the Pillars of Ashoka. According to S.P. Gupta, its style is unquestionably Achaemenid, seen in the tubular whiskers, although its mane is rather naturalistic. It is generally dated to around the 3rd century BCE.

Cunningham explained that at Bharhut the gateways carried Kharosthi letters, while the railings all had Indian markings. He concluded that the more artistically refined gateways were made by artists from the North, and the railings by local artists. The Bharhut gateway is dated to 100-75 BC, most probably 75 BC.

A stone palace at Kausambi, dated from the 8th century BCE to the 2nd century BCE, predates the Mauryan period. Its dressed stones were set in fine lime and coated with thick plaster, and it resembled a fortress with walls and towers. Its discovery discredits the theory that foreign influence lay behind the rise of Indian stone architecture.

war.text: The Kalinga War, ended around 261 BCE, was one of the largest and deadliest battles in Indian history. It was fought between the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka the Great and the kingdom of Kalinga on the east coast, and the article presumes the battle took place on the Dhauli hills. The war cost nearly 250,000 lives.

In May 326 BC, Alexander the Great fought Porus and the Pauravas at the Hydaspes River in what is now Punjab, Pakistan. The Macedonians won decisively and captured Porus, though it was possibly their most costly engagement. Arrian put Indian losses at 23,000, while Diodorus counted 12,000 dead and over 9,000 captured; two of Porus' sons and most of his chieftains were killed. Arrian gave Macedonian losses as a few hundred, but Diodorus reported 1000 killed, which J.F.C. Fuller saw as more realistic. Alexander spared Porus and made him a satrap, effectively reinstating him as ruler.

The world's first recorded military use of war elephants is in the Mahabharatha. From India, elephants were brought to the Persian Empire, where Darius III employed about 50 Indian elephants at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC against Alexander the Great.

Ashoka's own edicts record that after the Kalingans were conquered, 150,000 were deported, 100,000 were killed and many more died from other causes. Ashoka saw the bloodshed and felt that he was the cause of the destruction. He wrote that he felt deep remorse, and the savagery of the war led him to pledge never again to wage a war of conquest and to devote himself to dharma.

Alexander's march east would have led his army into a confrontation with the Nanda Empire, based in Magadha. According to Greek sources, the Nanda army was five times the size of the Macedonian army. His exhausted, homesick troops mutinied at the Hyphasis River and refused to advance.
war.source_title: Indian campaign of Alexander the Great

war.text: The Nanda Empire in northern and eastern India had an army of 6000 war elephants, 80,000 cavalry, 200,000 infantry and 8,000 armed chariots. Chanakya later wrote the Arthashastra on ancient Indian warfare, including the earliest uses of espionage and assassinations, and Chandragupta Maurya employed these techniques.

Some scholars argue Kalinga was a strategic threat to the Mauryas. It could interrupt communications between the Mauryan capital Pataliputra and possessions in the central Indian peninsula. Kalinga also controlled the coastline for trade in the Bay of Bengal.

To reach Porus' flank, Alexander found a crossing about 27 km upstream of his camp, where a wooded island divided the river. He left his general Craterus behind with most of the army to keep Porus from learning of the crossing. The plan was a classic pincer manoeuvre. A storm that night drowned out the sounds of the crossing. Porus sent his son, also named Porus, with a small cavalry and chariot force to fight them off, but the chariots were immobilized in mud, horse archers showered the force with arrows and heavy cavalry charged it. The young Porus' force was completely routed, and he died.

Porus ruled in Punjab and fielded a smaller army of 200 war elephants, 2,000 cavalry and 20,000 infantry at the Hydaspes. Alexander's larger army had 4,000 cavalry and 50,000 infantry. Porus presented great difficulty for it, though he was eventually defeated.

The Seleucid–Mauryan war of 305–303 BC ended with the Seleucids ceding vast eastern territories in exchange for 500 war elephants. This was a small part of the Mauryan forces, which included up to 9000 elephants by some accounts. The Seleucids used their new elephants at the Battle of Ipsus four years later.

According to Megasthenes, the Greek historian at the court of Chandragupta Maurya, the ruler of Kalinga had a powerful army of infantry, cavalry and elephants. Archaeologist Dilip K. Chakrabarti says the Mauryan army marched to Kalinga via Sarguja, a route later followed by Samudragupta.

The Macedonian army returned toward Persia through the Gedrosian Desert and Makran. Alexander's army took enormous casualties from hunger and thirst but fought no human enemy. Alexander refused as much water as possible, to share his men's sufferings and boost morale.
war.source_title: Indian campaign of Alexander the Great

literature.text: Sangam literature is the earliest known literature of South India. Most scholars place its historical era between about 300 BCE and 300 CE, while Kamil Zvelebil considers 100 BCE to 250 CE the most acceptable range.

The Mahābhārata is not just a single epic poem but a whole body of literature built around the heroic tales of the Bharata tribe, who are already mentioned in the Rigveda as a warlike tribe. Its core is a family feud in the royal house of the Kauravas, the descendants of Bharata, which leads to a bloody battle at Kurukshetra. Most of it was probably compiled between the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE by numerous authors, and its oldest preserved parts are not much older than around 400 BCE.

The earliest works of Indian literature were passed on orally. Classical Sanskrit literature developed rapidly during the first few centuries of the first millennium BCE, and so did the Pāli Canon and Tamil Sangam literature.

The Gupta script, used for writing Sanskrit, is associated with the Gupta Empire, a period of material prosperity and great religious and scientific developments. It descended from Brahmi and gave rise to the Nagari, Sarada and Siddham scripts, which in turn led to many of India's most important scripts.
literature.source_title: Ancient scripts of the Indian subcontinent

literature.text: Tamil legend links Sangam literature to three literary gatherings around Madurai and Kapāṭapuram. The first supposedly lasted over 4,440 years, the second over 3,700 years and the third over 1,850 years. Scholars regard this chronology as ahistorical and mythical.

The surviving Sangam collection includes the Tolkappiyam, the oldest surviving Tamil grammar. It also contains the Ettuttokai anthology, the Eight Collections, and the Pathuppaattu anthology, the Ten Songs.

The Mahabharata remains the longest single poem in the world. Historians once imagined an epic age for it and the Ramayana, but now recognise that the texts developed in stages over centuries. The existing texts are believed to date between c. 400 BCE and 400 CE.
The Numit Kappa, meaning Shooting at the Sun in Meitei, is an early Meitei epic. Its hero, Khwai Nungjeng Piba, shoots one of the two shining suns in the sky to create the night.

The Pallava dynasty of southern India, which existed from 275 CE to 897 CE, developed the Pallava script, from which Grantha ultimately took form. This script eventually gave rise to several Southeast Asian scripts, such as Khmer.

The Kharosthi script was used in Gandhara to write Gandhari Prakrit and Sanskrit, and it was also used in Central Asia. Introduced by at least the middle of the 3rd century BCE, it died out in its homeland around the 3rd century CE.
literature.source_title: Ancient scripts of the Indian subcontinent

literature.text: The Sangam collection contains 2381 poems in Tamil composed by 473 poets. Some 102 of those poets remain anonymous.
Sangam literature fell into oblivion for much of the second millennium CE. It was preserved in monasteries near Kumbakonam, where colonial-era scholars rediscovered it in the late nineteenth century.

Two Buddhist hymns by the poet Mātṛceṭa, who lived c. 70 to 150 CE, survive in Sanskrit. They are the Varṇārhavarṇa Stotra and the Satapancasataka, and they were very popular in the Buddhist community in India. Hymns said to be by Aśvaghoṣa are all lost.
After the Sangam period, great Tamil epics such as Cilappatikaram and Manimekalai were written. Silappatikaram used the akaval meter, a monologue style adopted from Sangam literature.

Sangam works glorified Murugan as the red god seated on the blue peacock, who is ever young and resplendent. The Tolkāppiyam gives his name as Murukaṉ, literally the youth, and the text mentions no Shaivism.

science.text: The Sushruta Samhita, an Ayurvedic text dated to the 6th century BCE in one account, contains 184 chapters. It describes 1120 illnesses, 700 medicinal plants, 64 preparations from mineral sources and 57 preparations based on animal sources.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The Sushruta Samhita by Sushruta, dated here to about 400 BC, has details about performing cataract surgery and plastic surgery. It is one of the milestones of Ayurveda, the ancient Indian system of medicine that mainly uses herbs as medicines.

In the 4th century BCE, the scholar Pāṇini made several discoveries in phonetics, phonology, and morphology. His morphological analysis remained more advanced than any equivalent Western theory until the mid-20th century.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Ancient Indian medical treatises such as the Charaka Samhita and the Sushruta Samhita stressed exercise as a way of avoiding conditions like diabetes. They prescribed exercise according to the seasons.

Ayurveda traces its origins to the Atharvaveda. By the time of the Buddha, around 520 BC, practitioners were commonly using mercuric-sulphur medicines, and Nagarjuna was an important practitioner of the period.

The Arthashastra of Kautilya mentions the construction of dams and bridges. Suspension bridges using plaited bamboo and iron chain were in use by about the 4th century, and rock-cut step wells date from 200 to 400 CE.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: In Southern India, in present-day Mysore, iron appeared as early as the 11th to 12th centuries BCE. Some scholars believe iron smelting was practiced on a bigger scale by the early 13th century BCE, suggesting the technology began even earlier.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The zinc mines of Zawar, near Udaipur in Rajasthan, were active during 400 BCE. Metal currency was also minted in India before the 5th century BCE, with coinage from 400 BCE to 100 CE made of silver and copper.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Some sources say leprosy was first described in the Sushruta Samhita. The Oxford Illustrated Companion to Medicine holds instead that the Atharvaveda, written in 1500 to 1200 BCE, described leprosy along with ritualistic cures for it.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: A palace excavated at Kausambi was built in six phases between the 8th century BCE and the 2nd century CE and used the principle of the true arch. Four-centered pointed arches spanned narrow passageways, segmental arches spanned wider areas, and part of the building formed a dome. The galleries and superstructure were found collapsed under a 5 cm thick layer of ash, which indicates the palace was destroyed by fire.

politics.text: Chandragupta Maurya defeated the Nanda dynasty and founded the Maurya Empire around 320 BCE. At its height under his grandson Ashoka, it briefly controlled the major urban hubs and arteries of the subcontinent, except the deep south.

When Alexander the Great invaded Punjab in 327 to 325 BCE, Greek sources described a great kingdom to the east whose army was five times the size of the Macedonian army. Modern historians identify its ruler as a Nanda king. Fear of that war, plus exhaustion, sparked a mutiny among Alexander's homesick soldiers and ended his Indian campaign.

The Gupta Empire lasted from the mid 3rd century to the mid 6th century CE and ruled much of the northern Indian subcontinent. Some historians call it the Golden Age of India, though others dispute that label.

The Kushan Empire, formed by the Yuezhi in the early 1st century CE, spread across parts of what is now Afghanistan, India and Pakistan. Its emperors were great patrons of Buddhism, and the long stability of their rule is sometimes described as Pax Kushana.

The last Nanda king, Dhana Nanda, was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya, supported by his mentor Chanakya. Ancient texts say the Nandas were unpopular because of their low-status birth, excessive taxation and general misconduct; Plutarch says the king was hated and despised by his subjects as wicked and of low origin. The Buddhist text Milinda Panha describes a war between the Nanda general Bhaddasala and Chandragupta that slaughtered 10,000 elephants, 100,000 horses, 5,000 charioteers and a billion foot soldiers. The article calls this an obvious exaggeration, but says it suggests the overthrow of the Nanda dynasty was a violent affair.

Chandragupta succeeded against Seleucus I, founder of the Seleucid Empire, in the Seleucid-Mauryan war of 305 BCE. Under the peace treaty negotiated in 303 BCE, the Mauryan Empire gained additional territory west of the Indus River.

Bindusara inherited a large empire at just 22 years old, according to Upinder Singh's dating of his accession. He extended it south as far as Karnataka and brought sixteen states under Mauryan rule; the medieval Tibetan scholar Taranatha says Chanakya helped him "destroy the nobles and kings of the sixteen kingdoms". He did not conquer the friendly Tamil kingdoms of the Cholas, Pandyas and Cheras, and only Kalinga remained outside his empire. His son Ashoka later conquered Kalinga in a furious war in which an estimated 100,000 soldiers and civilians were killed.

The Vedic Period in northern India, lasting from 1500 to 500 BCE, was marked by the composition of extensive collections of hymns called the Vedas. Its social structure was loosely stratified through the varna system, which was later incorporated into the present-day Jati system. At the end of the Rigvedic period this structure was characterised by the exclusion of some indigenous peoples, whose occupations were labelled impure.
The Ashokan Edicts mention the Cholas as one of the Mauryan Empire's southern neighbours. Although not subject to Ashoka, they were on friendly terms with him, according to Major Rock Edict No. 13.

Vasudeva Kanva began as a minister of the Shunga Emperor Devabhuti, then killed him and usurped the throne in 73 BCE. He allowed the kings of the Shunga dynasty to continue to rule in obscurity in a corner of their former dominions. The Kanva dynasty lasted until 28 BCE, and the Puranas suggest its last king was killed by Balipuccha, who founded the Andhra dynasty, though there is a lack of numismatical and archaeological evidence to support this.

The Chinese monk Faxian traveled through Gupta India during the reign of Chandragupta II, staying until 411 CE. He was pleased with the mildness of administration: the penal code was mild and offences were punished by fines only, and the king governed without decapitation or other corporal punishments. Yet he also recorded that even in cases of repeated attempts at wicked rebellion, criminals had their right hand cut off.

philosophy.text: Indian thinkers traditionally sorted their philosophies into six major Vedic schools: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā and Vedanta. Five major non-Vedic schools stood apart: Jain, Buddhist, Ajivika, Ajñana and Charvaka. The dividing line was often whether a school accepted the Vedas as a valid source of knowledge.

According to Diogenes Laërtius, the Greek philosopher Pyrrho accompanied Alexander the Great on his Indian campaign and developed his philosophy, now known as Pyrrhonism, in India. Christopher I. Beckwith finds it strikingly similar to the Buddhist three marks of existence, suggesting Pyrrho was influenced by contact with Buddhism.

Five of the eleven principal Upanishads were in all likelihood composed before the 6th century BCE. They contain the earliest mentions of yoga and moksha. The Upanishads summarise the philosophical portions of the Vedas and are commonly referred to as Vedānta.

Buddhism was founded by Gautama Siddhartha (563–483 BCE), who challenged the Vedic idea of a permanent self and proposed a path to liberate oneself from suffering. Jainism was founded by Mahavira (599–527 BCE), who emphasized non-violence and respect toward all forms of life.

The Arthashastra, attributed to the Mauryan minister Chanakya, is one of the early Indian texts devoted to political philosophy. Dated to the 4th century BCE, it discusses ideas of statecraft and economic policy.

The Nyāya school's foundational text, the Nyāya Sūtras, is credited to Aksapada Gautama and dated variously between the sixth and second centuries BCE. The school's most significant contributions were its systematic development of the theory of logic and methodology, and its treatises on epistemology.

Ahimsa, non-violence toward all beings, is mentioned in the Chandogya Upanishad (~800 BCE). By the mid 1st millennium BCE, Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism were all championing non-violence as an ethical value, and one that impacted one's rebirth.

The Indian Śramaṇa tradition had one of its earliest known prominent figures in Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankar, in the 9th century BCE. It became prominent in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, and even more so in the Mauryan period (c. 322–184 BCE). Later Indian philosophies either adopted ideas from Jainism and Buddhism or reacted against them.
The Kural, attributed to Valluvar and dated to around the 5th century CE, deals with ahimsa and morality. It extends them into political philosophy and love.

The Brahma Sutras of Badarayana, a Vedanta text completed in its surviving form around 400–450 CE, assume the existence of a text called Yoga Smriti. Its verses assert that the dualism of the prevailing Yoga philosophy is refuted, because Yoga's value lies in realizing the Self, not in propositions that conflict with the Vedic texts.

culture.text: The Vedic religion developed among Indo-Aryan peoples in the northwest of the subcontinent, in Punjab and the western Ganges plain. Its ideas and practices are preserved in the Vedic texts, and some Vedic rituals are still practised today. Those rituals included the Ashvamedha (horse sacrifice), the Pashubandhu (the annual or semi-annual animal sacrifice) and the Gomedha (cow sacrifice), and the dead were buried in graves or cremated.

Ancient India had many ball games and war-training activities, with both men and women taking part, and little or no equipment was used. Some specialist communities were known for acrobatic performances, such as dancing on bamboo.

Between about 800 and 200 BCE, traditional religious practices and beliefs in India were reassessed. According to Muesse, the Brahmins and the rituals they performed no longer enjoyed the same prestige they had held in the Vedic period.

The Shramana movement grew up alongside the Vedic tradition but separate from it, and often challenged Vedic and Upanishadic ideas of the soul (Atman) and ultimate reality (Brahman). In the 6th century BCE it matured into Jainism and Buddhism.

Non-violence, or ahimsa, is mentioned in the Chandogya Upanishad (about 800 BCE). By the middle of the 1st millennium BCE, Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism were all championing non-violence as an ethical value that affected one's rebirth.

Indian religions split into two broad branches: astika, which venerates the Veda, and nastika, which does not accept the Vedas as the only true source of knowledge. Even so, both branches shared the concepts of yoga, samsara (the cycle of birth and death) and moksha (liberation from that cycle).
By about 200 CE, feasting on animal slaughter was widely regarded as a form of violence against living beings. It became a religious and social taboo, an early root of India's vegetarian traditions.

Although cattle are sacred in modern Hinduism, there is historical evidence for the slaughter and eating of beef in ancient India. Historian Romila Thapar points to Vedic scriptures, ritual and cultural practice, while M. N. Srinivas argued that the beef taboo spread in the Vedic period as non-Aryans became 'Sanskritized' to raise their caste status.
